blocks.text: Jonah is commissioned to proclaim Jehovah’s word, yet the narrator never actually calls him a “prophet.” The chapter establishes his prophetic role through what he is sent to do rather than through a title.

Nineveh is called an exceedingly great city and associated with a three-day journey. That phrase need not describe the diameter of its excavated walled area; it may refer to the time needed for a visit, a wider district, or rhetorical language emphasizing the city’s greatness.

Jonah’s warning in verse 4 is only five Hebrew words. Its brevity sharpens the contrast with Nineveh’s sweeping response. The warning’s word for being “overthrown” may also suggest reversal, though readers debate whether the text intends both destruction and moral transformation as explicit meanings. The ruler remains unnamed, so attempts to identify him with a particular Assyrian king are speculative.

sections.title: A Brief Warning, an Expansive Response

blocks.text: The people believe, fast, wear sackcloth, and turn from evil and violence; even animals are included in the decree. These are the responses the story narrates, but interpreters differ over whether they represent conversion to Israel’s religion, ethical repentance, ritual humility, satire, or some combination. The animals make the response totalizing and perhaps comic, not a warrant for their deprivation or mistreatment. Verse 10 also raises a lasting question: the announced disaster is not carried out after Nineveh turns, while traditions differ over how to relate this narrative change to divine foreknowledge and immutability.

The chapter’s compassion toward Nineveh should not be read as excusing Assyrian imperial violence. Mercy and accountability are not presented as opposites, and the imagery of judgment does not license vengeance, collective punishment, or the dehumanization of enemies.

Jonah later became the haftarah, or public prophetic reading, for the Minḥah service of Yom Kippur. In living Jewish liturgy, this gives the book’s questions of repentance, mercy, justice, and resistance particular prominence.
